title: Pivot tables
examples: How do I use a pivot table to count things?
What is the difference between filtering and using a pivot table?
Can pivot tables handle dates in different years?

explain.say: A pivot table helps you summarise large amounts of data quickly.
You can summarise data by grouping similar items together easily.
Next, you can use filters to narrow down what you want to see.
For example, you could filter sales only for the North region.
Combining these lets you summarise only the North region sales.
In a job, you might summarise expense reports by department.

faq.q: What is the main difference between a pivot table and a simple sum formula?
faq.a: A pivot table automatically reorganises and summarises data based on categories you select. A simple sum formula requires you to manually specify every item you want to add up.
asks: How is it different from SUMIF?
Does it do the same as manual totalling?

faq.q: If I filter the data, does the pivot table update automatically?
faq.a: Yes, usually when you apply a filter, the pivot table updates to reflect only the visible data points. You might need to refresh the pivot table if the source data changes significantly.
asks: Will the summary change when I filter?
Do I have to manually tell it to update?

faq.q: Can I summarise data using multiple criteria at once?
faq.a: Absolutely, you can use multiple fields for both filtering and grouping. For example, you can summarise sales by region and then by product type.
asks: Can I group by two things?
What if I want to see Region AND Product?

faq.q: What if my raw data has missing values?
faq.a: Pivot tables usually treat missing values as zero or simply ignore them, depending on the calculation you choose. Always check your source data for blanks first.
asks: Does it break if some numbers are missing?

faq.q: Is it better to filter first or build the pivot table?
faq.a: It is often best to build the pivot table first using all data, and then apply filters to the pivot table itself for easier management.
asks: Should I filter the source or the table?

facts: Pivot tables are designed for summarising large datasets.
Filters allow you to restrict the data shown in a report.
You can summarise using counts, sums, averages, and more.
Always ensure your source data has clear headings.

quiz.say: You have sales data for three years and want to see the total sales for only the year 2022. Which tool should you use?

options.show: Apply a filter on the Year column.
options.say: Apply a filter on the Year column.

options.show: Build the pivot table and then manually delete the other years.
options.say: Build the pivot table and then manually delete the other years.

options.show: Use a simple SUM formula referencing only 2022 cells.
options.say: Use a simple SUM formula referencing only 2022 cells.

options.show: Sort the data by year and look at the total.
options.say: Sort the data by year and look at the total.

quiz.why: Filtering directly restricts the visible data to only the records matching 2022, which the pivot table then summarises.

wrong.1: This is time-consuming and risks missing data if you forget a year.
wrong.2: This is not scalable; you must manually select every single cell for the sum.
wrong.3: Sorting only changes the order; it does not hide the data for accurate summarising.

quiz.say: If you summarise sales by 'Region' and then want to see only 'East' and 'West', what is the most efficient method?

options.show: Sort the entire raw data set to put East and West together.
options.say: Sort the entire raw data set to put East and West together.

options.show: Use the filter function on the Region field.
options.say: Use the filter function on the Region field.

options.show: Create two separate pivot tables, one for East and one for West.
options.say: Create two separate pivot tables, one for East and one for West.

options.show: Manually adjust the row labels in the pivot table.
options.say: Manually adjust the row labels in the pivot table.

quiz.why: Filtering the region field tells the pivot table to only calculate summaries for those selected regions.

wrong.0: Sorting only rearranges the view; it does not change the summary calculation.
wrong.2: This creates redundant reports and is inefficient to manage.
wrong.3: This is prone to human error and does not reflect the underlying data change.

quiz.say: What is the primary purpose of using a pivot table?

options.show: To quickly aggregate and re-view large amounts of raw data.
options.say: To quickly aggregate and re-view large amounts of raw data.

options.show: To clean up inconsistent spelling in the source data.
options.say: To clean up inconsistent spelling in the source data.

options.show: To create a permanent, unchangeable record of the original data.
options.say: To create a permanent, unchangeable record of the original data.

options.show: To generate a complex, multi-page narrative report.
options.say: To generate a complex, multi-page narrative report.

quiz.why: The core function is taking many rows of detail and boiling them down into meaningful totals or averages.

wrong.1: Data cleaning requires dedicated text functions, not the pivot table feature.
wrong.2: Pivot tables are summaries; the original data remains untouched in the source sheet.
wrong.3: While they feed reports, their primary job is numerical summarisation, not narrative writing.
